newsitem.title: USA: Abortion pill maker breaks with U.S. distributor.
newsitem.headline: Abortion pill maker breaks with U.S. distributor.

text.p: The Hungarian drug company that had agreed to make the French abortion pill RU-486 for U.S. distribution has allegedly pulled out of the deal, court papers said on Thursday.
Danco Laboratories Ltd., the prospective distributor of the pill, said in a lawsuit filed in New York that Hungary's Chemical Works of Gedeon Richter Ltd broke off from the project this spring.
The pill has been available in Europe for several years. Although it was widely acclaimed by U.S. women's groups, it has been strongly opposed by anti-abortion groups.
The U.S. sponsor for the pill, the non-profit Population Council, said it was still talking with the manufacturer about the pill but was seeking other potential producers.
"This has been a very difficult process and it's had its ups and downs," said Sandra Waldman, a council spokeswoman. "We're in one of those cycles now and we keep going."

Danco filed suit in New York Supreme Court on May 9 seeking a court order to force Gedeon to continue the project. Gedeon's decision not to make RU-486 represented "a major and potentially ruinous setback" for the project, the suit said.
Danco said introduction of the pill could be put off for three to five years and meant losses of $200 million. Gedeon has received $500,000 for the project.

Gyorgy Thaler, Gedeon's director of development, told Danco in a Feb. 28 letter the company had "'elected to terminate the (manufacturing) agreement effective 12 months from this date,'" the suit said.

In the letter, Thaler wrote that because Gedeon had received no distribution forecasts from Danco, it was "under no obligation to supply the product during the (12-month) termination period, and Richter has therefore ceased all manufacturing activities with respect to the product.'"

Gedeon Richter also sent a letter on March 3 to Population Council President Margaret Catley-Carlson saying Gedeon Richter would end its agreement to make RU-486, effective 30 days after receipt of the letter.

Danco's suit is apparently the first public disclosure of the name of the Hungarian company. It had signed an agreement forbidding its identification, and a New York judge rejected on June 2 a petition that the court records be sealed.
A Washington lawyer for Gedeon, David Leitch, refused to comment about the suit. Tibor Simon, chief executive of Medipex of North America Inc, a Gedeon subsidiary, did not return a phone call.

RU-486 uses mifepristone to trigger abortions. It is a synthetic steroid that makes it difficult for a fertilised egg to adhere to the lining of the uterus. When taken with misoprotol, a drug that causes uterine contractions, the result is an abortion.

German chemicals and drugs group Hoechst AG said in April it was transferring all rights for the pill to a former manager and would stop making the drug completely, mainly because of adverse publicity.

Hoechst became linked to RU-486 when it acquired French drug company Roussel Uclaf. In the United States, Hoechst had already transferred the rights for the drug to the Population Council at the request of the U.S. government.
Danco is a Cayman Islands corporation 99 percent owned by NeoGen Investors LP, a California firm.
